chapters.title: Good Is the Enemy of Great
chapters.sourcePressure: The opening chapter frames good results as the trap that prevents a leap and grounds the book in comparative research: 11 good-to-great companies, matched comparisons, and sustained performance over time.
chapters.coreMove: Expose comfortable adequacy as a decision to stop investigating what greatness would require.
chapters.commonMisread: Greatness comes from one heroic breakthrough or from wanting excellence more intensely.
mustUseTerms: good is the enemy of great
mustNotDriftInto: later chapter frameworks as if already proved

chapters.title: Level 5 Leadership
chapters.sourcePressure: This chapter defines Level 5 leadership as the paradox of personal humility and fierce professional will, contrasted with celebrity leadership and anchored by the window-and-mirror pattern around credit and blame.
chapters.coreMove: Shift leadership from personal display to institution-first responsibility.
chapters.commonMisread: Humility means being mild, passive, or low-confidence.

chapters.title: First Who... Then What
chapters.sourcePressure: This chapter reverses the usual sequence: get the right people on the bus before fixing the destination, because the right people create adaptability and seat fit matters as much as raw talent.
chapters.coreMove: Resolve people fit before locking strategy so the organization can adapt without coercion.
chapters.commonMisread: This is ordinary hiring advice or permission to perform toughness.

chapters.title: Confront the Brutal Facts
chapters.sourcePressure: The chapter pairs clear-eyed reality with the Stockdale paradox: question-led leadership, debate, autopsies without blame, and red-flag mechanisms make truth hearable without collapsing resolve.
chapters.coreMove: Build a room where hard facts can enter without becoming despair or blame.
chapters.commonMisread: Candor means harshness, or faith means pretending the facts are better than they are.

chapters.title: The Hedgehog Concept
chapters.sourcePressure: The chapter centers the three-circle intersection of best-at capability, economic engine, and deep passion, emphasizing disciplined noes and realism developed over time.
chapters.coreMove: Find the narrow concept where capability, economics, and genuine commitment reinforce one another.
chapters.commonMisread: The Hedgehog Concept is a branding tagline or simple focus exercise.

chapters.title: A Culture of Discipline
chapters.sourcePressure: This chapter links disciplined people with freedom inside a clear framework, warning that bureaucracy often compensates for weak fit or unclear concepts and that stop-doing choices matter.
chapters.coreMove: Replace control-heavy management with disciplined freedom inside a clear concept.
chapters.commonMisread: Discipline means tighter supervision, more rules, or generic productivity habits.

chapters.title: Technology Accelerators
chapters.sourcePressure: Technology is presented as an accelerator of a disciplined concept already in motion, not the root cause of greatness and not a response to fear, prestige, or frenzy.
chapters.coreMove: Judge a tool by whether it accelerates the concept, not by its novelty or status.
chapters.commonMisread: The chapter is anti-technology or a general innovation playbook.

chapters.title: The Flywheel and the Doom Loop
chapters.sourcePressure: The chapter contrasts cumulative aligned pushes with reactive resets, showing that breakthrough is compounding momentum rather than a single event.
chapters.coreMove: Protect aligned momentum from the impulse to reset whenever progress is not yet dramatic.
chapters.commonMisread: Be patient and never change anything.

chapters.title: From Good to Great to Built to Last
chapters.sourcePressure: The closing chapter connects the leap to the harder question of durability, integrating disciplined people, disciplined thought, disciplined action, and cumulative momentum without importing unfrozen Built to Last frameworks.
chapters.coreMove: Turn a performance leap into institutional habits that can survive success.
chapters.commonMisread: Winning once proves the organization is permanently great.
